# The Puzzle of Integrable Impurities and the All-or-Nothing Theorem {#sec-lec1-all-or-nothing}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false title="What You Will Learn and Calculate in This Lecture"}
- **Conserved Charges Across an Impurity:** Why a boundary at $x=0$ can only preserve parity-even combinations $Q_s + Q_{-s}$, whereas a line defect at $x=0$ can preserve both chiralities $Q_{+s}$ and $Q_{-s}$ separately—and why conserving momentum forbids reflection.
- **The Delfino–Mussardo–Simonetti No-Go Theorem:** How to reduce a two-particle state $A_a(\theta_1)A_b(\theta_2)D$ in the Reflection–Transmission algebra along two spacetime paths and prove that in any interacting integrable theory, a defect is either *purely reflecting* or *purely transmitting*.
- **The Free-Fermion Escape Hatch:** How reflection and transmission coexist in the Ising model ($S=-1$) with a line of modified energy bonds, and how tuning the defect coupling decouples the line into two boundaries.
- **The Three Faces of the Triangle Relation:** How to translate between the index form, the braid form, and the quantum $L$-operator ($RTT$) form of the defect Yang–Baxter equation without ever getting lost in tensor-slot bookkeeping.
- **The Doubling Trick:** How folding the right half-line onto the left half-line turns any defect into a boundary in a doubled theory, and how this immediately dictates the laws of defect unitarity, defect crossing, and the defect bootstrap.
:::

---

## Setting the Stage: What Happens When an Integrable World Meets a Seam? {#sec-lec1-kinematics}

In Parts I–VI of the book, we studied integrable quantum field theories on the infinite line $x \in (-\infty, \infty)$. The hallmark of these theories is an infinite tower of local conserved charges $Q_s$ of higher spin $s$, which forbid particle production and force every multi-particle collision to factorize into a sequence of two-body scatterings governed by the Yang–Baxter equation (see the book: [Higher conserved charges and factorization](book:sec-factorization)).

In Part VII (see the book: [Integrable scattering with a boundary](book:sec-boundary-scattering)), we cut space in half and placed a wall at $x=0$. Now we want to do something less violent: we keep the entire line $x \in (-\infty, \infty)$, with a bulk field $\vec{\phi}(x,t)$ on the left half-line $x < 0$ and a bulk field $\vec{\psi}(x,t)$ on the right half-line $x > 0$, and we sew them together along a seam—a **line defect**—at $x=0$.

At first sight, you might think a defect is just a milder version of a boundary: when a particle hits $x=0$, part of its wave is reflected with amplitude $R(\theta)$ and part is transmitted with amplitude $\mathbb{T}(\theta)$. In ordinary one-dimensional quantum mechanics with a potential barrier $V(x) = g\,\delta(x)$, that is indeed what happens.

In an interacting integrable quantum field theory, however, we are about to discover that **partial reflection and partial transmission cannot coexist**. To understand why, let us begin by asking which bulk conserved charges can survive the presence of a seam at $x=0$.

### Blackboard Calculation 1: Flux Jumps and Surviving Charges {#sec-lec1-flux-jump}

Recall from the book's section [Higher conserved charges and factorization](book:sec-factorization) that in the bulk of a $(1+1)$-dimensional integrable field theory, a conserved charge $Q_s$ of spin $s$ comes from a local continuity equation. In light-cone coordinates $x^\pm = t \pm x$, with derivatives $\partial_\pm = \partial_t \pm \partial_x$, a spin-$s$ conservation law takes the form
$$
\partial_- T_{s+1} = \partial_+ \Theta_{s-1} \qquad (\text{for } Q_{+s}), \qquad
\partial_+ T_{-s-1} = \partial_- \Theta_{-s+1} \qquad (\text{for } Q_{-s}).
$$
Let us translate the first of these into standard $(t,x)$ coordinates. Using $\partial_- = \partial_t - \partial_x$ and $\partial_+ = \partial_t + \partial_x$, we have
$$
(\partial_t - \partial_x) T_{s+1} = (\partial_t + \partial_x) \Theta_{s-1}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\partial_t \underbrace{\big(T_{s+1} - \Theta_{s-1}\big)}_{\text{charge density }\rho_s}
= \partial_x \underbrace{\big(T_{s+1} + \Theta_{s-1}\big)}_{\text{flux }J_s}.
$$ {#eq-lec1-continuity}
When there is a defect at $x=0$, the fields $\vec{\phi}$ (on $x<0$) and $\vec{\psi}$ (on $x>0$) obey bulk equations of motion on their respective half-lines, but they may jump discontinuously at $x=0$. The total bulk charge is the sum of the integrals over the two half-lines:
$$
Q_s(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{0^-} \rho_s(\vec{\phi})\,dx + \int_{0^+}^{\infty} \rho_s(\vec{\psi})\,dx.
$$
Let us differentiate $Q_s(t)$ with respect to time and use (-@eq-lec1-continuity), assuming as usual that fields vanish at spatial infinity $x \to \pm\infty$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dQ_s}{dt}
&= \int_{-\infty}^{0^-} \partial_x J_s(\vec{\phi})\,dx + \int_{0^+}^{\infty} \partial_x J_s(\vec{\psi})\,dx \\
&= \Big[J_s(\vec{\phi})\Big]_{-\infty}^{0^-} + \Big[J_s(\vec{\psi})\Big]_{0^+}^{\infty} \\
&= J_s(0^-, t) - J_s(0^+, t).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-lec1-dqdt}
Look closely at (-@eq-lec1-dqdt): the rate of change of the bulk charge $Q_s$ is simply the **jump in the current flux** across the defect at $x=0$.

When can we build a conserved charge for the combined bulk-plus-defect system? Precisely when this flux jump is a **total time derivative** of some function $\Sigma_s$ localized at $x=0$:
$$
J_s(0^-, t) - J_s(0^+, t) = -\frac{d}{dt}\Sigma_s\big(\vec{\phi}(0^-,t), \vec{\psi}(0^+,t), \dots\big)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{d}{dt}\big(Q_s + \Sigma_s\big) = 0.
$$ {#eq-lec1-defect-charge}

Now compare a **boundary** with a **defect**:

1. **At a boundary ($x \le 0$):** There is no right half-line ($J_s(0^+,t) = 0$). On a single asymptotic particle of mass $m_a$ and rapidity $\theta$, the chiral charges act as $Q_{+s}|\theta\rangle = \chi_a^{(s)} e^{s\theta}|\theta\rangle$ and $Q_{-s}|\theta\rangle = \chi_a^{(s)} e^{-s\theta}|\theta\rangle$. Because a boundary reflects an incoming right-mover ($\theta > 0$) into an outgoing left-mover ($-\theta < 0$), any conserved charge at a boundary must assign the same eigenvalue to $|\theta\rangle$ and $|-\theta\rangle$. Since $e^{s\theta} \neq e^{-s\theta}$ for $\theta \neq 0$, neither $Q_{+s}$ nor $Q_{-s}$ can survive on its own; only the parity-even combination
   $$
   \tilde{Q}_s = Q_{+s} + Q_{-s} + \Sigma_s, \qquad \tilde{Q}_s|\theta\rangle = 2\chi_a^{(s)}\cosh(s\theta)|\theta\rangle,
   $$
   can be conserved (see the book: [Kinematics on the half-line](book:sec-half-line-kinematics)). In particular, for $s=1$, energy $E = \frac{1}{2}(Q_{+1} + Q_{-1})$ is conserved, while momentum $P = \frac{1}{2}(Q_{+1} - Q_{-1})$ is broken.

2. **At a defect ($x \in \mathbb{R}$):** A particle of rapidity $\theta$ arriving from $x<0$ does *not* have to bounce back into $x<0$; it can pass into $x>0$ keeping its rapidity $\theta$! Therefore, at a defect, the chiral charges $Q_{+s} + \Sigma_{+s}$ and $Q_{-s} + \Sigma_{-s}$ **can survive separately**.

What happens when they do? Let us prove our first fundamental result (which expands the book's [Elastic scattering off a defect](book:prp-defect-elastic)).

::: {#prp-lec1-elastic}
## Kinematics of Elastic Defect Scattering and Absence of Reflection {.unnumbered}
**[Established]** Suppose that infinitely many odd-spin charges $Q_s + Q_{-s} + \Sigma_s$ survive the defect with non-zero one-particle eigenvalues $\chi_a^{(s)}$, and that the internal states $|\alpha\rangle$ of the defect have a discrete energy spectrum $\{e_\alpha\}$. Then:

1. **Elasticity and Factorization:** Scattering off the defect is purely elastic—an $N$-particle in-state with rapidities $\{\theta_1, \dots, \theta_N\}$ goes into an $N$-particle out-state in which each particle is either reflected ($\theta_i \to -\theta_i$) or transmitted ($\theta_i \to +\theta_i$), changing its species label only within an equal-mass multiplet, and the $N$-particle amplitude factorizes into two-body bulk scatterings and single-particle defect reflections and transmissions [@delfino_mussardo_simonetti1994; @cafg2002].
2. **Momentum Conservation Forbids Reflection:** If, in addition, the spin-$\pm 1$ charges $Q_{+1} + \Sigma_{+1}$ and $Q_{-1} + \Sigma_{-1}$ survive *separately*—so that both a modified energy $E + E_d$ and a modified momentum $P + P_d$ are conserved—and the defect states have discrete momenta $\{p_\alpha\}$, then **every reflection amplitude vanishes identically ($R = 0$)**.
:::

::: {.proof}
For (1), when asymptotic wavepackets are far from $x=0$ (as $t \to \pm\infty$), the localized defect term $\Sigma_s$ contributes only a constant eigenvalue belonging to the discrete defect state $|\alpha\rangle$. For a single particle of rapidity $\theta > 0$ hitting the defect in state $|\alpha\rangle$ and emerging as particles with rapidities $\{\theta'_j\}$ while the defect transitions to $|\beta\rangle$, conservation of energy ($s=1$) gives
$$
m_a\cosh\theta + e_\alpha = \sum_j m_{b_j}\cosh\theta'_j + e_\beta.
$$
As we vary $\theta$ continuously while $e_\beta - e_\alpha$ takes values in a discrete set, differentiation with respect to $\theta$ (and applying the higher-spin charges $\sum_j \chi_{b_j}^{(s)}\cosh(s\theta'_j) = \chi_a^{(s)}\cosh(s\theta)$ for infinitely many odd $s$, just as in [the book's argument for a boundary](book:prp-boundary-elastic)) forces a single outgoing particle of the same mass $m_b = m_a$ with $\cosh\theta' = \cosh\theta$, hence $\theta' = +\theta$ (transmission to $x>0$) or $\theta' = -\theta$ (reflection to $x<0$), and $e_\beta = e_\alpha$. Using localized wavepackets shifted by higher-spin charges $e^{i\epsilon_s (Q_s + Q_{-s} + \Sigma_s)}$ separates multi-particle collisions in spacetime and yields factorization.

For (2), suppose a particle of mass $m$ and rapidity $\theta > 0$ arriving from the left is reflected back to the left with rapidity $-\theta$, while the defect transitions from $|\alpha\rangle$ to $|\beta\rangle$. Conservation of energy $E = \frac{1}{2}(Q_{+1}+Q_{-1}+\Sigma_{+1}+\Sigma_{-1})$ and momentum $P = \frac{1}{2}(Q_{+1}-Q_{-1}+\Sigma_{+1}-\Sigma_{-1})$ requires
$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Energy:} \quad m\cosh\theta + e_\alpha &= m\cosh(-\theta) + e_\beta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e_\beta - e_\alpha = 0,\\
\text{Momentum:} \quad m\sinh\theta + p_\alpha &= m\sinh(-\theta) + p_\beta \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_\beta - p_\alpha = 2m\sinh\theta.
\end{aligned}
$$
The right-hand side $2m\sinh\theta$ varies continuously with the incoming rapidity $\theta \in (0, \infty)$, whereas the left-hand side $p_\beta - p_\alpha$ belongs to a discrete set of differences of defect eigenvalues! A continuous function cannot take values in a discrete set except at isolated points, and by meromorphicity of the reflection amplitude in $\theta$, the reflection amplitude must vanish identically.
:::

---

## The Reflection–Transmission Algebra and the All-or-Nothing Theorem {#sec-lec1-rt-nogo}

What if we *do not* assume momentum conservation from the start? Suppose we only assume that the defect preserves the parity-even combinations $Q_s + Q_{-s} + \Sigma_s$ (just like a boundary does), so that single-particle reflection $R(\theta)$ and transmission $\mathbb{T}(\theta)$ are both kinematically allowed. Can a defect in an interacting integrable theory both reflect and transmit?

To answer this, Delfino, Mussardo, and Simonetti [@delfino_mussardo_simonetti1994] introduced an algebraic language extending the Zamolodchikov–Faddeev (ZF) algebra of the book's section [Higher conserved charges and factorization](book:sec-factorization). Let us set it up carefully.

### The Defect Zamolodchikov–Faddeev Algebra {#sec-lec1-zf-setup}

Recall that in the bulk, asymptotic particles are created by operators $A_a(\theta)$ satisfying the bulk exchange relation (see [the book](book:eq-zf-algebra)):
$$
A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2) = S_{ab}^{cd}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,A_d(\theta_2)\,A_c(\theta_1),
$$ {#eq-lec1-bulk-zf}
where we always write operators in **spatial order from left to right**:
- In an **in-state** (at $t \to -\infty$), the fastest right-moving particle is farthest to the left, so rapidities decrease from left to right: $\theta_1 > \theta_2 > \dots > \theta_N$.
- In an **out-state** (at $t \to +\infty$), the fastest right-moving particle has overtaken all slower ones and is farthest to the right, so rapidities increase from left to right: $\theta_1 < \theta_2 < \dots < \theta_N$.

Now insert a formal operator $D_\alpha$ at $x=0$ representing the defect in internal state $|\alpha\rangle \in \mathcal{W}$. Every state of the system is written with particles on the left half-line ($x<0$) placed to the **left** of $D_\alpha$, and particles on the right half-line ($x>0$) placed to the **right** of $D_\alpha$:

* **Incoming particle from the left ($x<0$):** A particle of rapidity $\theta > 0$ starts to the left of the defect, so the in-state is $A_a(\theta)\,D_\alpha$. After hitting the defect at $x=0$, it can either bounce back to $x<0$ with rapidity $-\theta < 0$ (now moving away from the defect on the left, so written $A_b(-\theta)\,D_\beta$) or pass through to $x>0$ with rapidity $+\theta > 0$ (now moving away from the defect on the right, so written $D_\beta\,A_b(\theta)$).
* **Incoming particle from the right ($x>0$):** A particle moving towards $x=0$ from the right has negative rapidity $-\theta < 0$ (with $\theta > 0$), so the in-state is $D_\alpha\,A_a(-\theta)$. After hitting the defect, it either bounces back to $x>0$ with rapidity $+\theta > 0$ ($D_\beta\,A_b(\theta)$) or transmits to $x<0$ with rapidity $-\theta < 0$ ($A_b(-\theta)\,D_\beta$).

Writing these two processes as algebraic exchange relations gives the **defect Zamolodchikov–Faddeev algebra** (see [the book](book:eq-defect-zf)) [@delfino_mussardo_simonetti1994; @cafg2002]:
$$
\begin{aligned}
A_a(\theta)\,D_\alpha &= R_{a\alpha}^{b\beta}(\theta)\,A_b(-\theta)\,D_\beta + \mathbb{T}_{a\alpha}^{\beta b}(\theta)\,D_\beta\,A_b(\theta),\\
D_\alpha\,A_a(-\theta) &= \bar{R}_{\alpha a}^{\beta b}(\theta)\,D_\beta\,A_b(\theta) + \bar{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha a}^{b\beta}(\theta)\,A_b(-\theta)\,D_\beta,
\end{aligned}
\qquad (\theta > 0).
$$ {#eq-lec1-defect-zf}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Index Convention Tip: Spatial Order Never Lies!"}
Notice how the indices on $R, \mathbb{T}, \bar{R}, \bar{\mathbb{T}}$ are arranged in (-@eq-lec1-defect-zf):
- **Lower indices** are the incoming labels, in left-to-right spatial order: $a\alpha$ for a particle hitting the defect from the left ($A_a D_\alpha$), and $\alpha a$ for a particle hitting the defect from the right ($D_\alpha A_a$).
- **Upper indices** are the outgoing labels, again in left-to-right spatial order: $b\beta$ when the outgoing particle is on the left ($A_b D_\beta$), and $\beta b$ when the outgoing particle is on the right ($D_\beta A_b$).

If you always keep indices in spatial order, you will never misplace a matrix multiplication!
:::

### Warm-Up Calculation: Single-Particle Unitarity {#sec-lec1-rt-unitarity}

Before we scatter two particles off the defect, let us see what happens when we apply (-@eq-lec1-defect-zf) twice to a single particle, assuming meromorphic continuation from $\theta > 0$ to $-\theta$. To keep the algebra transparent, consider first a single particle species and a defect with no internal states ($\mathcal{W} = \mathbb{C}$), so $R, \mathbb{T}, \bar{R}, \bar{\mathbb{T}}$ are scalar functions:
$$
A(\theta)\,D = R(\theta)\,A(-\theta)\,D + \mathbb{T}(\theta)\,D\,A(\theta), \qquad
D\,A(-\theta) = \bar{R}(\theta)\,D\,A(\theta) + \bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta)\,A(-\theta)\,D.
$$
Start with $A(\theta)\,D$, apply the first relation, and then expand $A(-\theta)\,D$ and $D\,A(\theta)$ on the right-hand side by analytically continuing the two relations to $-\theta$:
$$
\begin{aligned}
A(\theta)\,D
&= R(\theta)\,\Big[R(-\theta)\,A(\theta)\,D + \mathbb{T}(-\theta)\,D\,A(-\theta)\Big] \\
&\quad + \mathbb{T}(\theta)\,\Big[\bar{R}(-\theta)\,D\,A(-\theta) + \bar{\mathbb{T}}(-\theta)\,A(\theta)\,D\Big] \\
&= \Big[R(\theta)\,R(-\theta) + \mathbb{T}(\theta)\,\bar{\mathbb{T}}(-\theta)\Big] A(\theta)\,D
+ \Big[R(\theta)\,\mathbb{T}(-\theta) + \mathbb{T}(\theta)\,\bar{R}(-\theta)\Big] D\,A(-\theta).
\end{aligned}
$$
Since $A(\theta)\,D$ and $D\,A(-\theta)$ are linearly independent states, their coefficients must be $1$ and $0$:
$$
R(\theta)\,R(-\theta) + \mathbb{T}(\theta)\,\bar{\mathbb{T}}(-\theta) = 1, \qquad
R(\theta)\,\mathbb{T}(-\theta) + \mathbb{T}(\theta)\,\bar{R}(-\theta) = 0.
$$ {#eq-lec1-rt-unitarity}
Doing the same starting from $D\,A(-\theta)$ gives $\bar{R}(\theta)\bar{R}(-\theta) + \bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta)\mathbb{T}(-\theta) = 1$ and $\bar{R}(\theta)\bar{\mathbb{T}}(-\theta) + \bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta)R(-\theta) = 0$.

Equation (-@eq-lec1-rt-unitarity) looks completely familiar: if $\bar{R}(\theta) = R(-\theta)^*$ and $\bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta) = \mathbb{T}(-\theta)^*$ for real $\theta$, it is just the standard quantum-mechanical unitarity $|R(\theta)|^2 + |\mathbb{T}(\theta)|^2 = 1$ of a potential barrier! Nothing at the one-particle level warns us of the shock that awaits at the two-particle level.

### Blackboard Calculation 2: The Delfino–Mussardo–Simonetti No-Go Theorem {#sec-lec1-dms-proof}

Now let us send **two particles** from the left towards the defect at $x=0$, with rapidities $\theta_1 > \theta_2 > 0$. The in-state is
$$
|\text{in}\rangle = A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D.
$$
Suppose the bulk scattering on the left half-line is **diagonal**,
$$
A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2) = S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1),
$$
and suppose the defect has no internal states and preserves particle labels:
$$
A_a(\theta)\,D = R_a(\theta)\,A_a(-\theta)\,D + \mathbb{T}_a(\theta)\,D\,A_a(\theta).
$$

Because the ZF algebra is associative (which physically encodes **factorization**: shifting the relative positions of wavepackets changes the chronological order of two-body collisions without changing the final out-state), we can reduce $A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D$ to out-states in **two different ways** (@fig-lec1-histories; checked in `code/lectures/gemini_l1_f1_histories.py`):

![The two spacetime reduction orders for the two-particle in-state $A_a(\theta_1)A_b(\theta_2)D$ ($\theta_1 > \theta_2 > 0$) in the Delfino–Mussardo–Simonetti no-go theorem, showing how Mixed Channel A ($A_b(-\theta_2)DA_a(\theta_1)$) forces a head-on collision at relative rapidity $\theta_1 + \theta_2$ in Order I versus an overtaking collision at $\theta_1 - \theta_2$ in Order II.](figures/l1_histories.svg){#fig-lec1-histories width=92% fig-alt="Two-panel worldline diagram comparing Order I (particle b hits the defect D first) and Order II (particles a and b scatter in the bulk first) for the mixed reflection-transmission channel, illustrating why S(theta_1 + theta_2) = S(theta_1 - theta_2) is forced."}

Let us compute **every single step** of both reductions on the blackboard.

#### Reduction in Order I (Particle $b$ meets the defect first)
In the product $A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D$, the operator $A_b(\theta_2)$ stands immediately to the left of $D$. Apply the defect relation to $A_b(\theta_2)\,D$:
$$
A_a(\theta_1)\,\big(A_b(\theta_2)\,D\big)
= R_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D
+ \mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1)\,D\,A_b(\theta_2).
$$
Look at the two terms on the right-hand side. Neither is an out-state yet!

* In the **first term**, $A_a(\theta_1)$ (moving right) is to the left of $A_b(-\theta_2)$ (moving left), so they must cross each other in the bulk at rapidity difference $\theta_1 - (-\theta_2) = \theta_1 + \theta_2$:
  $$
  A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D = S_{ab}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1)\,D.
  $$
  Now $A_a(\theta_1)$ is adjacent to $D$, so it hits the defect:
  $$
  A_b(-\theta_2)\,\big(A_a(\theta_1)\,D\big)
  = R_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,A_a(-\theta_1)\,D
  + \mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D\,A_a(\theta_1).
  $$
  Notice that in $A_b(-\theta_2)\,A_a(-\theta_1)\,D$, both particles are moving left with $-\theta_1 < -\theta_2 < 0$, so the faster left-mover $a$ has still not overtaken $b$! Commuting them into out-state order ($-\theta_1$ to the left of $-\theta_2$) gives a factor $S_{ba}(-\theta_2 - (-\theta_1)) = S_{ba}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$:
  $$
  A_b(-\theta_2)\,A_a(-\theta_1)\,D = S_{ba}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,A_a(-\theta_1)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D.
  $$

* In the **second term**, $\mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1)\,D\,A_b(\theta_2)$, particle $a$ is adjacent to $D$, so it hits the defect:
  $$
  \big(A_a(\theta_1)\,D\big)\,A_b(\theta_2)
  = R_a(\theta_1)\,A_a(-\theta_1)\,D\,A_b(\theta_2)
  + \mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\,D\,A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2).
  $$
  In the last piece $D\,A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)$, both transmitted particles are on the right half-line with $\theta_1 > \theta_2 > 0$, so the faster particle $a$ overtakes $b$ on the right:
  $$
  D\,A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2) = S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,D\,A_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1).
  $$

Collecting all four out-states from **Order I**, we have:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\big[A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D\big]_{\text{Order I}}
&= \Big(R_b(\theta_2)\,S_{ab}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\,R_a(\theta_1)\,S_{ba}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\Big)\,A_a(-\theta_1)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D \\
&\quad + \Big(\mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\,S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\Big)\,D\,A_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1) \\
&\quad + \Big(R_b(\theta_2)\,S_{ab}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\Big)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D\,A_a(\theta_1) \\
&\quad + \Big(\mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2)\,R_a(\theta_1)\Big)\,A_a(-\theta_1)\,D\,A_b(\theta_2).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-lec1-order1}

#### Reduction in Order II (Particles $a$ and $b$ scatter in the bulk first)
Now start again from $A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D$, but first commute $A_a(\theta_1)$ past $A_b(\theta_2)$ in the bulk:
$$
\big(A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\big)\,D = S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1)\,D.
$$
Now $A_a(\theta_1)$ is adjacent to $D$, so we repeat the exact same steps as in Order I, but with $(a,\theta_1)$ and $(b,\theta_2)$ swapped! Writing out the result of expanding $A_b(\theta_2)\,(A_a(\theta_1)\,D)$ gives:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\big[A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D\big]_{\text{Order II}}
&= S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\bigg\{
\Big(R_a(\theta_1)\,S_{ba}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\,R_b(\theta_2)\Big)\,A_a(-\theta_1)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D \\
&\quad + \Big(\mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\,\mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2)\Big)\,D\,A_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1) \\
&\quad + \Big(\mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\,R_b(\theta_2)\Big)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D\,A_a(\theta_1) \\
&\quad + \Big(R_a(\theta_1)\,S_{ba}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2)\Big)\,A_a(-\theta_1)\,D\,A_b(\theta_2)
\bigg\},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-lec1-order2}
where in the both-reflected term $A_a(-\theta_1)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D$ and the both-transmitted term $D\,A_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1)$ the outgoing particles already emerged in the correct out-state spatial order ($-\theta_1 < -\theta_2$ on the left, $\theta_2 < \theta_1$ on the right), so no final bulk scattering occurred!

#### Comparing the Four Out-Channels
Equating the coefficients of the four linearly independent out-states in (-@eq-lec1-order1) and (-@eq-lec1-order2) gives us four equations:

1. **Both Reflected ($A_a(-\theta_1)\,A_b(-\theta_2)\,D$):**
   $$
   R_b(\theta_2)\,S_{ab}(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,R_a(\theta_1)\,S_{ba}(\theta_1-\theta_2)
   = S_{ab}(\theta_1-\theta_2)\,R_a(\theta_1)\,S_{ba}(\theta_1+\theta_2)\,R_b(\theta_2),
   $$
   which holds automatically in any parity-invariant diagonal theory ($S_{ab} = S_{ba}$).
2. **Both Transmitted ($D\,A_b(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1)$):**
   $$
   \mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\,S_{ab}(\theta_1-\theta_2)
   = S_{ab}(\theta_1-\theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\,\mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2),
   $$
   which is an identity for scalar functions!
3. **Mixed Channel A ($A_b(-\theta_2)\,D\,A_a(\theta_1)$, where $b$ reflects and $a$ transmits):**
   $$
   R_b(\theta_2)\,S_{ab}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)
   = S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\,R_b(\theta_2),
   $$
   or equivalently:
   $$
   R_b(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_a(\theta_1)\,\Big[S_{ab}(\theta_1 + \theta_2) - S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\Big] = 0.
   $$ {#eq-lec1-mixed-a}
4. **Mixed Channel B ($A_a(-\theta_1)\,D\,A_b(\theta_2)$, where $a$ reflects and $b$ transmits):**
   $$
   \mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2)\,R_a(\theta_1)
   = S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,R_a(\theta_1)\,S_{ba}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2),
   $$
   or equivalently:
   $$
   R_a(\theta_1)\,\mathbb{T}_b(\theta_2)\,\Big[1 - S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,S_{ba}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\Big] = 0.
   $$ {#eq-lec1-mixed-b}

Stop and stare at (-@eq-lec1-mixed-a) and (-@eq-lec1-mixed-b)! Why did this happen physically?

* In **Mixed Channel A**, along Order I, particle $b$ bounces off the defect first ($\theta_2 \to -\theta_2$) and then collides head-on with the incoming particle $a$ at relative rapidity $\theta_1 - (-\theta_2) = \theta_1 + \theta_2$. Along Order II, particle $a$ overtakes $b$ *before* reaching the defect at relative rapidity $\theta_1 - \theta_2$, passes through the defect, and then $b$ bounces off the defect into the empty left half-line without ever meeting $a$ again!
* Therefore, along Path I the two particles scatter at relative rapidity $\theta_1 + \theta_2$, whereas along Path II they scatter at relative rapidity $\theta_1 - \theta_2$!

Since meromorphic functions vanish on an open set only if one of the factors vanishes identically:

* If $R_b \not\equiv 0$ and $\mathbb{T}_a \not\equiv 0$, then (-@eq-lec1-mixed-a) forces $S_{ab}(\theta_1 + \theta_2) = S_{ab}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)$ for all $\theta_1 > \theta_2 > 0$, which means **$S_{ab}(\theta)$ must be a constant independent of rapidity**!
* If also $R_a \not\equiv 0$ and $\mathbb{T}_b \not\equiv 0$, then (-@eq-lec1-mixed-b) forces $S_{ab}(\theta_1-\theta_2)S_{ba}(\theta_1+\theta_2) = 1$. Setting $a=b$ gives $S_{aa}(\theta) = \text{const}$ and $S_{aa}^2 = 1$, hence **$S_{aa} = \pm 1$ (a free boson or free fermion)**!

We have just proved the book's [Pure reflection or pure transmission](book:prp-rt-nogo) in complete detail:

> **The All-or-Nothing Principle:** In any interacting integrable theory with a rapidity-dependent diagonal bulk $S$-matrix, an integrable defect without internal states **cannot both reflect and transmit**. Either $\mathbb{T}_a(\theta) \equiv 0$ (a purely reflecting defect, which is just two decoupled half-line boundaries back-to-back) or $R_a(\theta) \equiv 0$ (a **purely transmitting defect**, which conserves asymptotic momentum).

As explained in the book's section [Reflection, transmission and a no-go theorem](book:sec-rt-algebra), Castro-Alvaredo, Fring, and Göhmann [@cafg2002] extended this no-go theorem to non-diagonal bulk $S$-matrices and defects with internal states whenever the reflection and transmission matrices commute in the defect space within a single communicating sector. Thus, in interacting integrable field theories—such as sine-Gordon, sinh-Gordon, and affine Toda theories—integrable line defects are **purely transmitting**.

---

## The Free-Fermion Escape Hatch: The Ising Defect {#sec-lec1-ising}

Before we leave reflection behind forever, let us verify that when $S = -1$ (the massive Majorana fermion of the off-critical Ising model), the no-go theorem's escape hatch opens wide!

In the massive Ising model with $S(\theta) = -1$, both $S(\theta_1+\theta_2) - S(\theta_1-\theta_2) = (-1) - (-1) = 0$ and $1 - S(\theta_1-\theta_2)S(\theta_1+\theta_2) = 1 - (-1)^2 = 0$ hold identically! So Mixed Channels A and B impose *no restriction at all* on $R(\theta)$ and $\mathbb{T}(\theta)$.

What is left? Only the single-particle unitarity equations (-@eq-lec1-rt-unitarity) (with parity $\bar{R} = R$ and $\bar{\mathbb{T}} = \mathbb{T}$):
$$
R(\theta)R(-\theta) + \mathbb{T}(\theta)\mathbb{T}(-\theta) = 1, \qquad
R(\theta)\mathbb{T}(-\theta) + \mathbb{T}(\theta)R(-\theta) = 0,
$$ {#eq-lec1-ising-unitarity}
together with the crossing relation between reflection and transmission [@delfino_mussardo_simonetti1994, eq. (2.9)]:
$$
R(\theta) = \mathbb{T}\!\left(\frac{i\pi}{2} - \theta\right) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \mathbb{T}(\theta) = \mathbb{T}(i\pi - \theta), \quad R(\theta) = -R(i\pi - \theta) \text{ (up to conventions)}.
$$
Specifically, for a line defect of strength $g$ in the free Majorana fermion action (a line of modified energy bonds in the lattice Ising model), solving the Dirac equation across $x=0$ gives (see [the book](book:eq-defect-zf)) with [@delfino_mussardo_simonetti1994, eq. (3.5)]:
$$
\mathbb{T}(\theta) = \frac{\cos\chi\,\sinh\theta}{\sinh\theta - i\sin\chi}, \qquad
R(\theta) = \frac{i\sin\chi\,\cosh\theta}{\sinh\theta - i\sin\chi},
$$ {#eq-lec1-ising-rt}
where the angle $\chi$ is related to the defect coupling $g$ by
$$
\sin\chi = -\frac{g}{1 + g^2/4}, \qquad \cos\chi = \frac{1 - g^2/4}{1 + g^2/4}.
$$

Let us check (-@eq-lec1-ising-unitarity) on the blackboard right now:
$$
\begin{aligned}
R(\theta)R(-\theta) + \mathbb{T}(\theta)\mathbb{T}(-\theta)
&= \frac{(i\sin\chi\,\cosh\theta)(i\sin\chi\,\cosh\theta) + (\cos\chi\,\sinh\theta)(-\cos\chi\,\sinh\theta)}{(\sinh\theta - i\sin\chi)(-\sinh\theta - i\sin\chi)} \\
&= \frac{-\sin^2\chi\,\cosh^2\theta - \cos^2\chi\,\sinh^2\theta}{-\sinh^2\theta - \sin^2\chi} \\
&= \frac{\sin^2\chi\,(1 + \sinh^2\theta) + (1 - \sin^2\chi)\,\sinh^2\theta}{\sinh^2\theta + \sin^2\chi}
= \frac{\sin^2\chi + \sinh^2\theta}{\sinh^2\theta + \sin^2\chi} = 1,
\end{aligned}
$$
and for the off-diagonal unitarity relation:
$$
R(\theta)\mathbb{T}(-\theta) + \mathbb{T}(\theta)R(-\theta)
= \frac{(i\sin\chi\,\cosh\theta)(-\cos\chi\,\sinh\theta) + (\cos\chi\,\sinh\theta)(i\sin\chi\,\cosh\theta)}{-\sinh^2\theta - \sin^2\chi} = 0.
$$
Look at the physical limits of (-@eq-lec1-ising-rt), plotted in @fig-lec1-ising (`code/lectures/gemini_l1_f2_ising.py`):
- At $g = 0$ ($\chi = 0$): $\mathbb{T}(\theta) = 1$ and $R(\theta) = 0$ (no defect).
- At $g = \pm 2$ ($\cos\chi = 0$, $\sin\chi = \mp 1$): **transmission vanishes identically** ($\mathbb{T}(\theta) = 0$), and $R(\theta) = \mp\frac{i\cosh\theta}{\sinh\theta \pm i}$, which are the exact reflection amplitudes of the free and fixed boundary conditions of the half-line Ising model!

![The free-fermion Ising defect ($S = -1$): (a) transmission probability $|\mathbb{T}(\theta)|^2$ and reflection probability $|R(\theta)|^2 = 1 - |\mathbb{T}(\theta)|^2$ across couplings from $g=0$ (transparent) to $g=\pm 2$ (decoupled boundaries); (b) trajectory of the pole $\theta_p = i\chi(g)$ in the imaginary rapidity plane as $g$ varies.](figures/l1_ising.svg){#fig-lec1-ising width=92% fig-alt="Two-panel plot of the Ising free-fermion defect showing partial transmission and reflection probabilities in panel (a) and the bound-state/virtual-state pole trajectory theta_p = i*chi(g) in panel (b)."}

---

## Pure Transmission and the Three Faces of the Triangle Relation {#sec-lec1-triangle}

From now on, we set $R = \bar{R} = 0$ and study **purely transmitting defects** in interacting theories, where both bulk scattering $S_{ab}^{cd}$ and defect transmission $\mathbb{T}_{a\alpha}^{\beta b}$ can be non-diagonal matrices acting on the particle multiplet $V(\theta) = \mathrm{span}\{v_a\}$ and the defect space $\mathcal{W} = \mathrm{span}\{w_\alpha\}$:
$$
A_a(\theta)\,D_\alpha = \mathbb{T}_{a\alpha}^{\beta b}(\theta)\,D_\beta\,A_b(\theta), \qquad
D_\alpha\,A_a(-\theta) = \bar{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha a}^{b\beta}(\theta)\,A_b(-\theta)\,D_\beta.
$$ {#eq-lec1-pure-t}
As linear maps between tensor products (where **tensor order is always spatial order from left to right**), $\mathbb{T}$ and $\bar{\mathbb{T}}$ act as
$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{T}(\theta)&: V(\theta) \otimes \mathcal{W} \longrightarrow \mathcal{W} \otimes V(\theta),
&\qquad \mathbb{T}(\theta)(v_a \otimes w_\alpha) &= \sum_{\beta,b} \mathbb{T}_{a\alpha}^{\beta b}(\theta)\,w_\beta \otimes v_b,\\
\bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta)&: \mathcal{W} \otimes V(-\theta) \longrightarrow V(-\theta) \otimes \mathcal{W},
&\qquad \bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta)(w_\alpha \otimes v_a) &= \sum_{b,\beta} \bar{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha a}^{b\beta}(\theta)\,v_b \otimes w_\beta.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-lec1-t-maps}

In the literature on integrable defects, you will encounter the fundamental consistency equation for $\mathbb{T}(\theta)$—the **Triangle Relation** (or defect Yang–Baxter equation) [@konik_leclair1999; @bcz2005; @bajnok_george2006]—written in three seemingly different notations. Students often get tripped up translating between them. Let us derive all three side by side so that their equivalence is crystal clear (see the book: [Three forms of the triangle relation](book:prp-triangle-forms)).

### Blackboard Calculation 3: Deriving the Index, Braid, and RTT Forms {#sec-lec1-three-forms}

#### Form 1: The $S/\mathbb{T}$ Index Form
Start with the two-particle in-state $A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D_\alpha$ ($\theta_1 > \theta_2 > 0$) and reduce it to the out-state $D_\gamma\,A_e(\theta_2)\,A_f(\theta_1)$ along our two spacetime orders, keeping all matrix indices explicit:

* **Order II (scatter in the bulk first, then cross the defect):**
  1. Bulk scattering $A_a(\theta_1)A_b(\theta_2) = S_{ab}^{cd}(\theta_1-\theta_2)A_d(\theta_2)A_c(\theta_1)$ puts particle $c(\theta_1)$ adjacent to $D_\alpha$:
     $$
     A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D_\alpha = S_{ab}^{cd}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,A_d(\theta_2)\,A_c(\theta_1)\,D_\alpha.
     $$
  2. Particle $c(\theta_1)$ crosses $D_\alpha \to D_\beta$, emerging on the right as $f(\theta_1)$:
     $$
     = S_{ab}^{cd}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_{c\alpha}^{\beta f}(\theta_1)\,A_d(\theta_2)\,D_\beta\,A_f(\theta_1).
     $$
  3. Particle $d(\theta_2)$ crosses $D_\beta \to D_\gamma$, emerging on the right as $e(\theta_2)$:
     $$
     = S_{ab}^{cd}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_{c\alpha}^{\beta f}(\theta_1)\,\mathbb{T}_{d\beta}^{\gamma e}(\theta_2)\,D_\gamma\,A_e(\theta_2)\,A_f(\theta_1).
     $$

* **Order I (cross the defect first, then scatter on the right):**
  1. Particle $b(\theta_2)$ crosses $D_\alpha \to D_\beta$, emerging on the right as $d(\theta_2)$:
     $$
     A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D_\alpha = \mathbb{T}_{b\alpha}^{\beta d}(\theta_2)\,A_a(\theta_1)\,D_\beta\,A_d(\theta_2).
     $$
  2. Particle $a(\theta_1)$ crosses $D_\beta \to D_\gamma$, emerging on the right as $c(\theta_1)$:
     $$
     = \mathbb{T}_{b\alpha}^{\beta d}(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_{a\beta}^{\gamma c}(\theta_1)\,D_\gamma\,A_c(\theta_1)\,A_d(\theta_2).
     $$
  3. Since $\theta_1 > \theta_2$, the faster particle $c(\theta_1)$ overtakes $d(\theta_2)$ on the right via $A_c(\theta_1)A_d(\theta_2) = S_{cd}^{fe}(\theta_1-\theta_2)A_e(\theta_2)A_f(\theta_1)$:
     $$
     = \mathbb{T}_{b\alpha}^{\beta d}(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_{a\beta}^{\gamma c}(\theta_1)\,S_{cd}^{fe}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,D_\gamma\,A_e(\theta_2)\,A_f(\theta_1).
     $$

Equating the coefficients of $D_\gamma\,A_e(\theta_2)\,A_f(\theta_1)$ gives the **$S/\mathbb{T}$ index form of the Triangle Relation** (see [the book](book:eq-triangle-st)):
$$
S_{ab}^{cd}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_{c\alpha}^{\beta f}(\theta_1)\,\mathbb{T}_{d\beta}^{\gamma e}(\theta_2)
= \mathbb{T}_{b\alpha}^{\beta d}(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_{a\beta}^{\gamma c}(\theta_1)\,S_{cd}^{fe}(\theta_1 - \theta_2).
$$ {#eq-lec1-triangle-st}

#### Form 2: The Braid Form
In Part VI of the book (with [the intertwiner $\check R$](book:eq-r-check)), the bulk $S$-matrix is written as a braid operator $\check{S}(\theta_1-\theta_2) = \Phi_{\text{bulk}}(\theta_1-\theta_2)\,\check{R}(x_1/x_2): V(\theta_1)\otimes V(\theta_2) \to V(\theta_2)\otimes V(\theta_1)$ with matrix elements
$$
\check{S}(v_a \otimes v_b) = \sum_{c,d} S_{ab}^{cd}\,v_d \otimes v_c,
$$
where the output tensor factors are reversed to match the spatial exchange of the two particles.

Now look at the composite map from the initial space $V(\theta_1) \otimes V(\theta_2) \otimes \mathcal{W}$ (slots $1, 2, 3$) to the final space $\mathcal{W} \otimes V(\theta_2) \otimes V(\theta_1)$:

* Along **Order I** (acting from right to left as operators):
  1. First, $\mathbb{T}_{23}(\theta_2)$ acts on slots 2 and 3 ($V(\theta_2)\otimes\mathcal{W} \to \mathcal{W}\otimes V(\theta_2)$), taking $v_a \otimes v_b \otimes w_\alpha \mapsto \mathbb{T}_{b\alpha}^{\beta d}\,v_a \otimes w_\beta \otimes v_d$ in $V(\theta_1)\otimes\mathcal{W}\otimes V(\theta_2)$.
  2. Next, $\mathbb{T}_{12}(\theta_1)$ acts on slots 1 and 2 ($V(\theta_1)\otimes\mathcal{W} \to \mathcal{W}\otimes V(\theta_1)$), taking this to $\mathbb{T}_{b\alpha}^{\beta d}\,\mathbb{T}_{a\beta}^{\gamma c}\,w_\gamma \otimes v_c \otimes v_d$ in $\mathcal{W}\otimes V(\theta_1)\otimes V(\theta_2)$.
  3. Finally, $\check{S}_{23}(\theta_1-\theta_2)$ acts on slots 2 and 3 ($V(\theta_1)\otimes V(\theta_2) \to V(\theta_2)\otimes V(\theta_1)$), giving $\mathbb{T}_{b\alpha}^{\beta d}\,\mathbb{T}_{a\beta}^{\gamma c}\,S_{cd}^{fe}\,w_\gamma \otimes v_e \otimes v_f$—which is the right-hand side of (-@eq-lec1-triangle-st)!
* Along **Order II**:
  1. First, $\check{S}_{12}(\theta_1-\theta_2)$ swaps $V(\theta_1)\otimes V(\theta_2) \to V(\theta_2)\otimes V(\theta_1)$ in slots 1 and 2: $v_a \otimes v_b \otimes w_\alpha \mapsto S_{ab}^{cd}\,v_d \otimes v_c \otimes w_\alpha$.
  2. Next, $\mathbb{T}_{23}(\theta_1)$ moves $V(\theta_1)$ across $\mathcal{W}$ in slots 2 and 3: $\mapsto S_{ab}^{cd}\,\mathbb{T}_{c\alpha}^{\beta f}\,v_d \otimes w_\beta \otimes v_f$.
  3. Finally, $\mathbb{T}_{12}(\theta_2)$ moves $V(\theta_2)$ across $\mathcal{W}$ in slots 1 and 2: $\mapsto S_{ab}^{cd}\,\mathbb{T}_{c\alpha}^{\beta f}\,\mathbb{T}_{d\beta}^{\gamma e}\,w_\gamma \otimes v_e \otimes v_f$—the left-hand side of (-@eq-lec1-triangle-st)!

Since the bulk scalar factor $\Phi_{\text{bulk}}(\theta_1-\theta_2)$ appears once on each side, it cancels out, leaving the **braid form of the Triangle Relation** (see [the book](book:eq-triangle-braid)):
$$
\check{R}_{23}\!\left(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\right)\,\mathbb{T}_{12}(\theta_1)\,\mathbb{T}_{23}(\theta_2)
= \mathbb{T}_{12}(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_{23}(\theta_1)\,\check{R}_{12}\!\left(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\right).
$$ {#eq-lec1-triangle-braid}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="A Particle Is a Defect!"}
Compare (-@eq-lec1-triangle-braid) with the braid Yang–Baxter equation (see [the book](book:eq-ybe-braid)):
$$
\check{R}_{23}\!\left(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\right)\,\check{R}_{12}\!\left(\frac{x_1}{x_3}\right)\,\check{R}_{23}\!\left(\frac{x_2}{x_3}\right)
= \check{R}_{12}\!\left(\frac{x_2}{x_3}\right)\,\check{R}_{23}\!\left(\frac{x_1}{x_3}\right)\,\check{R}_{12}\!\left(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\right).
$$
They are the **exact same equation** if we choose $\mathcal{W} = V(\theta_d)$ ($x_3 = x(\theta_d)$) and $\mathbb{T}(\theta) = \check{R}(x(\theta)/x(\theta_d))$! Physically, a bulk particle sitting at rapidity $\theta_d$ is itself a purely transmitting defect [@bajnok_george2006].
:::

#### Form 3: The $RTT$ (Quantum $L$-Operator) Form
In the braid form (-@eq-lec1-triangle-braid), the three vector spaces $V(\theta_1)$, $V(\theta_2)$, and $\mathcal{W}$ keep swapping slots. What if we want each vector space to **stay in its own fixed tensor slot**—slot 1 for $V(\theta_1)$, slot 2 for $V(\theta_2)$, and slot 3 for $\mathcal{W}$?

We simply compose each braid operator with the permutation (flip) operator $P(u \otimes v) = v \otimes u$:
$$
R\left(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\right) = P\,\check{R}\left(\frac{x_1}{x_2}\right): V_1 \otimes V_2 \to V_1 \otimes V_2, \qquad
\mathbb{L}(\theta) = P\,\mathbb{T}(\theta): V \otimes \mathcal{W} \to V \otimes \mathcal{W}.
$$ {#eq-lec1-l-def}
Let us substitute $\check{R}_{ij} = P_{ij}R_{ij}$ and $\mathbb{T}_{ij} = P_{ij}\mathbb{L}_{ij}$ into (-@eq-lec1-triangle-braid) and push all permutation operators $P_{ij}$ to the left using the standard symmetric-group identity $P_{ij} X_{jk} = X_{ik} P_{ij}$:

* **Left-hand side of (-@eq-lec1-triangle-braid):**
  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \check{R}_{23}\,\mathbb{T}_{12}(\theta_1)\,\mathbb{T}_{23}(\theta_2)
  &= P_{23}\,R_{23}\,P_{12}\,\mathbb{L}_{12}(\theta_1)\,P_{23}\,\mathbb{L}_{23}(\theta_2) \\
  &= P_{23}\,P_{12}\,R_{13}\,\mathbb{L}_{12}(\theta_1)\,P_{23}\,\mathbb{L}_{23}(\theta_2)
  \qquad\text{(since $R_{23}P_{12} = P_{12}R_{13}$)} \\
  &= \underbrace{P_{23}\,P_{12}\,P_{23}}_{=\,P_{13}}\,R_{12}\,\mathbb{L}_{13}(\theta_1)\,\mathbb{L}_{23}(\theta_2).
  \end{aligned}
  $$
* **Right-hand side of (-@eq-lec1-triangle-braid):**
  $$
  \begin{aligned}
  \mathbb{T}_{12}(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{T}_{23}(\theta_1)\,\check{R}_{12}
  &= P_{12}\,\mathbb{L}_{12}(\theta_2)\,P_{23}\,\mathbb{L}_{23}(\theta_1)\,P_{12}\,R_{12} \\
  &= P_{12}\,P_{23}\,\mathbb{L}_{13}(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{L}_{23}(\theta_1)\,P_{12}\,R_{12}
  \qquad\text{(since $\mathbb{L}_{12}P_{23} = P_{23}\mathbb{L}_{13}$)} \\
  &= \underbrace{P_{12}\,P_{23}\,P_{12}}_{=\,P_{13}}\,\mathbb{L}_{23}(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{L}_{13}(\theta_1)\,R_{12}.
  \end{aligned}
  $$

Cancelling the overall permutation $P_{13}: V_1 \otimes V_2 \otimes \mathcal{W} \to \mathcal{W} \otimes V_2 \otimes V_1$ from both sides gives the **$RTT$ form of the Triangle Relation** (see [the book](book:eq-triangle-rtt)):
$$
R_{12}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,\mathbb{L}_{13}(\theta_1)\,\mathbb{L}_{23}(\theta_2)
= \mathbb{L}_{23}(\theta_2)\,\mathbb{L}_{13}(\theta_1)\,R_{12}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)
\qquad\text{on } V(\theta_1) \otimes V(\theta_2) \otimes \mathcal{W}.
$$ {#eq-lec1-triangle-rtt}

This equation is a revelation [@bajnok_george2006]: if we view $\mathbb{L}(\theta)$ as a $\dim V \times \dim V$ matrix whose entries $\mathbb{L}_a^{\ b}(\theta)$ are operators acting on the defect space $\mathcal{W}$,
$$
\mathbb{L}_a^{\ b}(\theta)\,w_\alpha = \sum_\beta \mathbb{T}_{a\alpha}^{\beta b}(\theta)\,w_\beta,
$$
then (-@eq-lec1-triangle-rtt) is **Faddeev's $RLL$ relation** [@faddeev1980; @faddeev_takhtajan1987] defining the Yang–Baxter algebra of $R$! Every integrable defect transmission matrix is a **quantum $L$-operator** whose auxiliary space is the particle multiplet $V(\theta)$ and whose quantum space is the defect Hilbert space $\mathcal{W}$. In Lecture 4 (@sec-lec4-quantum-groups), this insight will connect defects directly to Baxter's $Q$-operators.

---

## The Doubling Trick: A Defect Is a Boundary in Disguise {#sec-lec1-doubling}

How do we find the crossing symmetry and bootstrap equations for a transmitting defect? In their early papers, Delfino, Mussardo, and Simonetti [@delfino_mussardo_simonetti1994] and Konik and LeClair [@konik_leclair1999] simply postulated defect crossing by analogy with bulk crossing. In 2006, Bajnok and George [@bajnok_george2006] showed that you do not need to guess: **every defect theory on the full line can be folded into a boundary theory on the left half-line**, so that all defect axioms follow mathematically from the boundary axioms of Part VII (see the book: [Integrable scattering with a boundary](book:sec-boundary-scattering))!

### How the Folding Works {#sec-lec1-folding-map}

Take our field $\vec{\phi}(x,t)$ on $x \le 0$ and our field $\vec{\psi}(x,t)$ on $x \ge 0$, and define a doubled field $\Phi(x,t)$ living solely on the left half-line $x \le 0$ (see the book: [The doubling trick](book:sec-doubling-trick)):
$$
\Phi(x,t) = \big(\vec{\phi}(x,t),\,\vec{\psi}(-x,t)\big), \qquad x \le 0.
$$ {#eq-lec1-doubled-field}
Let us trace carefully what this mirror map $x \mapsto -x$ does to the particles of the $\vec{\psi}$-theory:

1. **Kinematics:** A $\vec{\psi}$-particle at $x > 0$ moving to the right with rapidity $\theta > 0$ becomes a particle of the second copy $V'$ at $-x < 0$ moving to the *left* with rapidity $-\theta < 0$. Conversely, an incoming $\vec{\psi}$-particle at $x > 0$ moving towards the defect with rapidity $-\theta < 0$ becomes an incoming $V'$-particle at $-x < 0$ moving towards the boundary $x=0$ with positive rapidity $+\theta > 0$!
2. **One-Particle Space:** The single-particle Hilbert space of the doubled bulk theory on $x \le 0$ is the direct sum
   $$
   M(\theta) = V(\theta) \oplus V'(\theta),
   $$
   where $V(\theta)$ carries the $\vec{\phi}$-particles and $V'(\theta)$ is a copy of $V(-\theta)$ carrying the mirrored $\vec{\psi}$-particles.
3. **Bulk $S$-Matrix of the Doubled Theory:**
   - Two $V$-particles scatter with the original braid $S$-matrix $\check{S}_{VV}(\theta_1-\theta_2) = \check{S}(\theta_1-\theta_2)$.
   - Because $\vec{\phi}(x)$ on $x<0$ and $\vec{\psi}(-x)$ on $x>0$ live in different halves of space and never touch outside $x=0$, a $V$-particle and a $V'$-particle pass right through each other without interacting! In braid notation (where passing through with amplitude $1$ simply swaps their spatial slots), $\check{S}_{VV'} = P$ and $\check{S}_{V'V} = P$.
   - What about two $V'$-particles? Because the mirror map $x \mapsto -x$ **reverses spatial order** (the particle farther to the right on $x>0$ becomes farther to the left on $x<0$), two $V'$-particles scatter with the parity-conjugate braid matrix $\check{S}_{V'V'}(\theta_1-\theta_2) = P\,\check{S}(\theta_1-\theta_2)\,P$!
4. **The Doubled Reflection Matrix $K(\theta)$:**
   When a $V$-particle (a $\vec{\phi}$-particle from $x<0$) hits the boundary $x=0$ and is transmitted into $x>0$ by $\mathbb{T}(\theta): V(\theta)\otimes\mathcal{W} \to \mathcal{W}\otimes V(\theta)$, in the folded picture it bounces back into $x<0$ as a $V'$-particle! To keep the boundary space $\mathcal{W}$ on the right of the particle space (as in Part VII's convention $K(\theta): M(\theta)\otimes\mathcal{W} \to M(-\theta)\otimes\mathcal{W}$), we compose $\mathbb{T}(\theta)$ with the flip $P$:
   - $V(\theta)\otimes\mathcal{W} \xrightarrow{\mathbb{T}(\theta)} \mathcal{W}\otimes V(\theta) \xrightarrow{P} V'(-\theta)\otimes\mathcal{W}$,
   - $V'(\theta)\otimes\mathcal{W} \xrightarrow{P} \mathcal{W}\otimes V(-\theta) \xrightarrow{\bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta)} V(-\theta)\otimes\mathcal{W}$.

   Therefore, for a purely transmitting defect, the boundary reflection matrix of the doubled theory is purely block off-diagonal (see [the book](book:eq-doubled-k); illustrated in @fig-lec1-doubling and checked in `code/lectures/gemini_l1_f3_doubling.py`) [@bajnok_george2006, eq. (10)]:
   $$
   K(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta)\,P \\[3pt] P\,\mathbb{T}(\theta) & 0 \end{pmatrix}
   \qquad \text{acting on } \big(V(\theta) \oplus V'(\theta)\big) \otimes \mathcal{W}.
   $$ {#eq-lec1-doubled-k}

![The doubling (folding) trick: (a) transmission through a defect at $x=0$ on the full line $x \in \mathbb{R}$; (b) folding the right half-line $x > 0$ onto $x < 0$ via $\tilde{\psi}(x,t) = \psi(-x,t)$ turns left-to-right and right-to-left transmissions into species-converting reflections $V \leftrightarrow V'$ off the doubled boundary $K(\theta)$.](figures/l1_doubling.svg){#fig-lec1-doubling width=92% fig-alt="Two-panel schematic comparing unfolded transmission through a defect at x=0 with the folded half-line boundary theory on x<=0 where the reflection matrix K(theta) is block off-diagonal between V and V'."}

### Blackboard Calculation 4: Reading Defect Unitarity and Crossing off the Doubled Boundary {#sec-lec1-doubling-calc}

Let us now plug the block matrix (-@eq-lec1-doubled-k) into the standard boundary axioms of the book's chapter [Integrable scattering with a boundary](book:sec-boundary-scattering) and watch the defect axioms fall into our lap (see the book: [The doubling trick](book:prp-doubling))!

#### 1. Defect Unitarity from Boundary Unitarity
Boundary unitarity (see [the book](book:eq-boundary-unitarity)) states that $K(-\theta)\,K(\theta) = 1_{(V\oplus V')\otimes\mathcal{W}}$. Multiplying the $2\times 2$ block matrices gives
$$
K(-\theta)\,K(\theta)
= \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \bar{\mathbb{T}}(-\theta)\,P \\[3pt] P\,\mathbb{T}(-\theta) & 0 \end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix} 0 & \bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta)\,P \\[3pt] P\,\mathbb{T}(\theta) & 0 \end{pmatrix}
= \begin{pmatrix} \bar{\mathbb{T}}(-\theta)\,P^2\,\mathbb{T}(\theta) & 0 \\[3pt] 0 & P\,\mathbb{T}(-\theta)\,\bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta)\,P \end{pmatrix}.
$$
Since $P^2 = 1$, setting this equal to $\begin{pmatrix} 1_{V\otimes\mathcal{W}} & 0 \\ 0 & 1_{V'\otimes\mathcal{W}} \end{pmatrix}$ immediately yields **defect unitarity** (see [the book](book:eq-defect-unitarity)):
$$
\bar{\mathbb{T}}(-\theta)\,\mathbb{T}(\theta) = 1_{V\otimes\mathcal{W}}, \qquad
\mathbb{T}(-\theta)\,\bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta) = 1_{\mathcal{W}\otimes V}.
$$ {#eq-lec1-defect-unitarity}

#### 2. Defect Crossing from Boundary Crossing-Unitarity
Recall from the book's section [Boundary unitarity and crossing-unitarity](book:sec-boundary-unitarity-crossing) that Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov boundary crossing-unitarity ([the book's equation](book:eq-boundary-crossing-unitarity)) is the statement that a boundary can emit a virtual particle–antiparticle pair at rapidities $\frac{i\pi}{2} - \theta$ and $\frac{i\pi}{2} + \theta$, and that this pair amplitude is invariant under bulk scattering $\check{S}(2\theta)$ of the two emitted particles:
$$
K_{B\bar{A}}\!\left(\frac{i\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \sum_{C,D} \check{S}_{CD}^{AB}(2\theta)\,K_{D\bar{C}}\!\left(\frac{i\pi}{2} + \theta\right),
$$
where capital indices $A, B \in V \oplus V'$ label the doubled particle space and we suppress defect indices for a moment (they are carried along as spectators on $\mathcal{W}$).

Now choose $A = a \in V$ (a $\vec{\phi}$-particle) and $B = b' \in V'$ (a mirrored $\vec{\psi}$-particle). What is the bulk scattering $\check{S}_{CD}^{ab'}(2\theta)$ between a $V$-particle and a $V'$-particle in the doubled theory? As we saw above, the two copies **do not interact in the bulk**! So $\check{S}(2\theta)$ on a mixed pair simply flips their slots with amplitude $1$: the only non-zero term on the right-hand side is $C = b' \in V'$ and $D = a \in V$, with $\check{S}_{b'a}^{ab'}(2\theta) = 1$!

Therefore, for the mixed block between $V$ and $V'$, the bulk $S$-matrix at $2\theta$ drops out completely, leaving
$$
K_{b'\bar{a}}\!\left(\frac{i\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = K_{a\bar{b}'}\!\left(\frac{i\pi}{2} + \theta\right).
$$
Now let us restore the defect labels $\alpha, \beta$ and read off the matrix elements from (-@eq-lec1-doubled-k):
- The lower-left block $K_{b'\bar{a}}$ maps $\bar{a} \in V$ and incoming defect state $\alpha$ to $b' \in V'$ and outgoing defect state $\beta$, which is $\mathbb{T}_{\bar{a}\alpha}^{\beta b}$.
- The upper-right block $K_{a\bar{b}'}$ maps $\bar{b}' \in V'$ and incoming defect state $\alpha$ to $a \in V$ and outgoing defect state $\beta$, which is $\bar{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha\bar{b}}^{a\beta}$.

Replacing $\frac{i\pi}{2} - \theta$ by $\theta$ (so $\frac{i\pi}{2} + \theta$ becomes $i\pi - \theta$) and relabelling $\bar{a} \to a$ gives the **defect crossing relation** (see [the book](book:eq-defect-crossing)) [@bajnok_george2006, eq. (15)]:
$$
\mathbb{T}_{a\alpha}^{\beta b}(\theta) = \bar{\mathbb{T}}_{\alpha\bar{b}}^{\,\bar{a}\beta}(i\pi - \theta).
$$ {#eq-lec1-defect-crossing}

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" title="Physical Meaning of Defect Crossing"}
Look at (-@eq-lec1-defect-crossing): analytically continuing the incoming particle $a(\theta)$ on the left by $\theta \to i\pi - \theta$ turns it into an outgoing antiparticle $\bar{a}$ on the left, and turns the outgoing particle $b$ on the right into an incoming antiparticle $\bar{b}$ arriving from the right at rapidity $-(i\pi - \theta)$! The defect state transition $\alpha \to \beta$ is untouched because the defect line itself is not crossed—only the particle worldline is rotated by $90^\circ$ in Euclidean spacetime.

In the simplest case of a single self-conjugate particle ($\bar{a} = a$) and a defect with no internal states ($\mathcal{W} = \mathbb{C}$), defect unitarity (-@eq-lec1-defect-unitarity) and defect crossing (-@eq-lec1-defect-crossing) read
$$
\mathbb{T}(\theta)\,\bar{\mathbb{T}}(-\theta) = 1, \qquad
\mathbb{T}(\theta) = \bar{\mathbb{T}}(i\pi - \theta)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\mathbb{T}(\theta)\,\mathbb{T}(\theta + i\pi) = 1.
$$ {#eq-lec1-scalar-unitarity-crossing}
Notice how much simpler (-@eq-lec1-scalar-unitarity-crossing) is than boundary crossing-unitarity $K(\theta)K(\theta+i\pi) = S(2\theta + i\pi)$: because the two half-lines do not interact in the bulk of the doubled theory, there is no $S(2\theta)$ factor!
:::

---

## Defect Bound States, the Bootstrap, and Defects on a Circle {#sec-lec1-bootstrap-circle}

Let us complete our toolkit of general defect axioms with two essential physical constructions (see the book: [Defect bound states and the bootstrap](book:sec-defect-bound-states), [Defects on the circle](book:sec-defect-circle)).

### 1. The Defect Bootstrap vs. The Boundary Bootstrap {#sec-lec1-bootstrap}

Suppose a particle $a$ arriving from the left with imaginary rapidity $\theta = iu$ in the **physical strip** $0 < u < \frac{\pi}{2}$ (where the particle energy $E = m_a\cos u$ lies between $0$ and $m_a$) produces a simple pole in $\mathbb{T}_a^\alpha(\theta)$. This signals that particle $a$ can be absorbed by the defect in state $|\alpha\rangle$ to form an **excited defect bound state** $|\beta\rangle$ of energy
$$
e_\beta = e_\alpha + m_a\cos u.
$$
How does a second particle $b(\theta)$ transmit across this excited defect $|\beta\rangle$?

Think of $|\beta\rangle$ as the original defect $|\alpha\rangle$ with particle $a(iu)$ sitting just to its right (the side to which $a$ was transmitted). When particle $b(\theta)$ crosses from left to right, it first crosses the bare defect $|\alpha\rangle$ and then scatters **once** past the bound particle $a(iu)$! In a diagonal theory, this gives the **defect bound-state bootstrap** (see [the book](book:eq-defect-bootstrap)) [@bajnok_simon2008]:
$$
\mathbb{T}_b^\beta(\theta) = S_{ba}(\theta - iu)\,\mathbb{T}_b^\alpha(\theta), \qquad
\bar{\mathbb{T}}_b^\beta(\theta) = S_{ab}(\theta + iu)\,\bar{\mathbb{T}}_b^\alpha(\theta).
$$ {#eq-lec1-defect-bootstrap}
Similarly, if a bulk particle $c$ is a bound state of bulk particles $a(\theta + i\bar{u}_{ac}^b)$ and $b(\theta - i\bar{u}_{bc}^a)$ formed at a pole of $S_{ab}$, then $c$ crosses the defect simply by letting its two constituents cross at their respective rapidities:
$$
\mathbb{T}_c(\theta) = \mathbb{T}_a\!\left(\theta + i\bar{u}_{ac}^b\right)\,\mathbb{T}_b\!\left(\theta - i\bar{u}_{bc}^a\right).
$$ {#eq-lec1-bulk-bootstrap}

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Why the Defect Bootstrap Has Half as Many Factors as the Boundary Bootstrap"}
Compare (-@eq-lec1-defect-bootstrap) and (-@eq-lec1-bulk-bootstrap) with the boundary bootstrap equations of Part VII of the book ([first](book:eq-boundary-bootstrap) and [second](book:eq-boundary-bootstrap-bulk)):
- At a **boundary**, a reflected particle $b$ passes the bound particle $a(iu)$ *twice*—once on the way in ($\theta - iu$) and once on the way out ($\theta + iu$), giving $K_b^\beta(\theta) = S_{ba}(\theta-iu)S_{ab}(\theta+iu)K_b^\alpha(\theta)$. At a **defect**, the transmitted particle keeps moving right and never comes back, so it meets $a(iu)$ **only once**!
- Likewise, when a composite particle $c = (ab)$ reflects off a boundary, its two constituents $a$ and $b$ cross *each other* once as their order reverses upon reflection, producing an extra bulk factor $S_{ab}(\theta + i\bar{u}_{ac}^b - (-\theta + i\bar{u}_{bc}^a))$. When $c = (ab)$ transmits through a defect, both constituents keep moving in the same direction at the same velocity and **never cross each other**, so (-@eq-lec1-bulk-bootstrap) is a pure product of two transmission factors!
:::

### 2. Wrapping a Defect Around a Circle and Twist Defects {#sec-lec1-circle}

Finally, what happens if we put our $(1+1)$-dimensional theory on a spatial circle of circumference $L$, with a purely transmitting defect at $x=0$?

* **Defect sitting at $x=0$ (running along time):** When we carry particle $j$ of rapidity $\theta_j$ once around the circle from $x=0^+$ to $x=L \equiv 0^-$, it scatters past all other $N-1$ particles and then crosses the defect from left to right via $\mathbb{T}(\theta_j)$. For a diagonal theory with $\mathcal{W}=\mathbb{C}$, periodicity of the wavefunction gives the **defect Bethe–Yang equations**:
  $$
  e^{i m_j L \sinh\theta_j}\,\mathbb{T}_{a_j}(\theta_j)\,\prod_{k \neq j} S_{a_j a_k}(\theta_j - \theta_k) = 1, \qquad j = 1, \dots, N.
  $$ {#eq-lec1-bethe-yang}
* **Defect running around the circle at fixed time (90° rotation):** If we rotate Euclidean spacetime by $90^\circ$, the defect line runs around the spatial circle at a fixed time slice, so it acts as a quantum operator $\hat{D}$ on the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_L$ of the circular theory! Because the defect conserves energy and momentum, $\hat{D}$ commutes with the bulk Hamiltonian and momentum: $[\hat{D}, H] = [\hat{D}, P] = 0$. When $\mathcal{W}$ has internal states, every particle on the circle crosses the defect line once while the defect state propagates around the ring, so $\hat{D}$ is the **trace over $\mathcal{W}$ of a product of $L$-operators**—a transfer matrix with auxiliary space $\mathcal{W}$!

The simplest transmitting defect of all has no rapidity dependence whatsoever: if each particle carries a conserved topological charge vector $\mu_a$, then setting $\mathcal{W} = \mathbb{C}$ and
$$
\mathbb{T}_a(\theta) = e^{i\alpha\cdot\mu_a}, \qquad \bar{\mathbb{T}}_a(\theta) = e^{-i\alpha\cdot\mu_a}
$$ {#eq-lec1-twist-defect}
trivially satisfies the Triangle Relation (since the bulk $S$-matrix conserves $\mu_a + \mu_b$), defect unitarity ($e^{i\alpha\cdot\mu_a}e^{-i\alpha\cdot\mu_a} = 1$), and defect crossing (since the antiparticle has $\mu_{\bar{a}} = -\mu_a$, so $\bar{\mathbb{T}}_{\bar{a}}(i\pi-\theta) = e^{-i\alpha\cdot(-\mu_a)} = e^{i\alpha\cdot\mu_a} = \mathbb{T}_a(\theta)$). Plugging (-@eq-lec1-twist-defect) into (-@eq-lec1-bethe-yang) simply multiplies the periodicity condition by the Bloch phase $e^{i\alpha\cdot\mu_j}$ (see the book: [Twist defects](book:prp-twist-defect)): **a Bloch twist on a circle is nothing other than the invertible topological symmetry line of the topological charge!**

In the next lecture, we will leave abstract scattering axioms behind and ask: *how can a local classical field theory possibly create a defect that conserves momentum and transmits waves and solitons with zero reflection?*

---

## Guided Rediscovery Exercises {#sec-lec1-exercises}

To cement the skills of this lecture, work through the following three problems by hand.

::: {#exr-lec1-mixed-channel}
### Problem 1.1: The Mixed Defect Triangle Relation
In @sec-lec1-three-forms we reduced $A_a(\theta_1)\,A_b(\theta_2)\,D_\alpha$ with both particles arriving from the left. Now consider the in-state $A_a(\theta_1)\,D_\alpha\,A_b(-\theta_2)$ ($\theta_1, \theta_2 > 0$), where particle $a$ arrives from the left and particle $b$ arrives from the right, and the defect is purely transmitting ($R = \bar{R} = 0$).

1. Reduce $A_a(\theta_1)\,D_\alpha\,A_b(-\theta_2)$ to the out-state $A_e(-\theta_2)\,D_\gamma\,A_f(\theta_1)$ in two ways: (i) let $a$ cross the defect first, then scatter with $b$ on the right, and then let $b$ cross to the left; (ii) let $b$ cross the defect first, scatter with $a$ on the left, and then let $a$ cross to the right.
2. Write down the resulting consistency equation relating $\mathbb{T}(\theta_1)$, $\bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_2)$, and $S(\theta_1 + \theta_2)$.
3. Using defect unitarity $\bar{\mathbb{T}}(\theta_2) = \mathbb{T}(-\theta_2)^{-1}$, show that this mixed equation is automatically satisfied whenever the Triangle Relation (-@eq-lec1-triangle-braid) holds for all rapidities!
:::

::: {#exr-lec1-cdd}
### Problem 1.2: Defect CDD Factors and "Half a Particle"
In a theory with a single self-conjugate particle ($\bar{a} = a$) and a state-independent defect ($\mathcal{W} = \mathbb{C}$), a **defect CDD factor** is a meromorphic function $\Phi_d(\theta)$ satisfying unitarity and crossing (-@eq-lec1-scalar-unitarity-crossing):
$$
\Phi_d(\theta)\,\Phi_d(\theta + i\pi) = 1, \qquad \bar{\Phi}_d(\theta) = \Phi_d(i\pi - \theta) = \frac{1}{\Phi_d(-\theta)}.
$$
1. Verify that the function
   $$
   \mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(\theta) = -i\,\frac{\sinh\!\big(\frac{\theta - \theta_d}{2} - \frac{i\pi}{4}\big)}{\sinh\!\big(\frac{\theta - \theta_d}{2} + \frac{i\pi}{4}\big)}
   = \frac{e^{-(\theta - \theta_d)} + i}{e^{-(\theta - \theta_d)} - i}
   $$
   satisfies $\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(\theta)\,\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(\theta + i\pi) = 1$ and $|\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(\theta)| = 1$ for real $\theta$ and $\theta_d$, but is *not* parity invariant: $\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(\theta)\,\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(-\theta) \neq 1$.
2. Compute its square $\big[\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(\theta)\big]^2$ and the square of its inverse $\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}_{\rm odd}(\theta) = \mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(\theta)^{-1}$, and show that they equal the standard bulk CDD blocks
   $$
   \big[\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(\theta)\big]^2 = f_{-1/2}(\theta - \theta_d) = \frac{\sinh(\theta - \theta_d) - i}{\sinh(\theta - \theta_d) + i}, \qquad
   \big[\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}_{\rm odd}(\theta)\big]^2 = f_{1/2}(\theta - \theta_d) = \frac{\sinh(\theta - \theta_d) + i}{\sinh(\theta - \theta_d) - i},
   $$
   which satisfy the bulk unitarity and crossing equations $f(\theta)f(-\theta) = 1$ and $f(\theta) = f(i\pi - \theta)$! Why can a single bulk particle never have $\mathbb{T}^{\rm cl}(\theta)$ as its bulk $S$-matrix, whereas a defect can?
:::

::: {#exr-lec1-doubled-re}
### Problem 1.3: The Doubled Reflection Equation Block by Block
Write out the braid Reflection Equation (see [the book](book:eq-reflection-braid)) for the doubled theory on $M(\theta_1) \otimes M(\theta_2) \otimes \mathcal{W}$,
$$
K_{23}(\theta_2)\,\check{S}_{12}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\,K_{23}(\theta_1)\,\check{S}_{12}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)
= \check{S}_{12}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)\,K_{23}(\theta_1)\,\check{S}_{12}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)\,K_{23}(\theta_2),
$$
where $K(\theta)$ is the off-diagonal block matrix (-@eq-lec1-doubled-k) and $\check{S}$ acts as $\check{S}$ on $V\otimes V$, as $P\check{S}P$ on $V'\otimes V'$, and as the flip $P$ on $V\otimes V'$ and $V'\otimes V$. Restrict both sides to an incoming state in $V(\theta_1) \otimes V(\theta_2) \otimes \mathcal{W}$ (which must emerge in $V'(-\theta_1) \otimes V'(-\theta_2) \otimes \mathcal{W}$ after two off-diagonal reflections) and verify step-by-step that this block of the Reflection Equation is identical to the braid Triangle Relation (-@eq-lec1-triangle-braid)!
:::
